source.title: No Free Lunch From Random Feature Ensembles
source.authors: Benjamin S. Ruben; W. Tong; H. Chaudhry; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests random-feature ridge regression (RFRR) risk as feature count and sample size change, and argues that non-monotonicity in this setting can result from a non-optimally tuned ridge parameter.
record.gate_note: The paper reports monotonicity results for optimally tuned ridge and says risk may increase at a particular fixed ridge value. It does not report an epoch sweep or a test of whether label noise produces, splits, or removes a peak. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper's main subject is ensemble allocation. Its Theorem 4.1 and Figure 1/S3 experiments still bear on the claim. They show that test risk of random-feature ridge regression is monotone in sample size P and feature count N when the ridge is optimally tuned, and may rise at fixed ridge. The authors argue that such violations come from overfitting at non-optimal ridge. This bears on V6 (the peak vanishes under optimal regularization) and qualifies V3 and V4 in a non-deep model class.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The main conclusion is a 'no free lunch' theorem: at optimal ridge, a single large RFRR model beats any ensemble with the same total feature count, and near-optimal ensemble scaling depends on task structure. On double descent specifically, they conclude that violations of 'more is better' in RFRR arise only from overfitting at non-optimal ridge.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes random-feature ridge regression ensembles with theoretical risk estimates and ReLU random features, rather than training deep networks and sweeping their size, epochs, or sample size as in the original double-descent studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Ridge choice changes the reported behavior: risk may increase at a particular fixed ridge value but decreases monotonically when ridge is optimally tuned.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed total feature count, ridge-optimized risk increases monotonically with ensemble size K; a single large model is optimal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Splitting a fixed parameter budget into an ensemble never beats a single model at optimal ridge.

record.problems: The experiments concern random-feature models and binarized classification tasks, not trained deep networks. The analysis adopts a Gaussian universality assumption; the paper notes that dimension-free deterministic equivalence has not been proven for ensembled RFRR. Several reported curves are not numerically tabulated.

untested.parts: No deep networks; only random-feature ridge regression.
Location of any sample-wise peak relative to the interpolation threshold (P≈N) is not reported.
Other model classes; the shape and location of the fixed-ridge curve around the interpolation point.
Degrees of freedom are used analytically, but no test of whether one complexity measure predicts peak locations.
Role of label noise or variance in driving the peak; multiple or triple descent.

missing.what: Figure 1 and S3 plot risk at non-optimal λ values against P and N. These curves would show where any non-monotonic bump sits relative to P=N, but the values are not extracted or stated in the text.

record.verdict_notes: The monotonicity theorem extends Simon et al. (2023) to ensembles. All evidence on the claim is either theoretical (deterministic equivalents under Gaussian universality) or stated qualitatively from figures without numbers. The record's V4 'challenges' label is replaced with limits_scope: monotone descent at optimal ridge does not contradict improvement past interpolation, it only removes the rise.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses random-feature ridge regression, not deep networks whose learned model size is swept.
No test-error trajectory over training epochs is reported.
The reported monotonicity result concerns optimally tuned ridge; the paper does not locate a sample-size peak near an interpolation threshold.
The study tests RFRR, not a range of model classes, and does not report a full fall-rise-fall curve around an interpolation point.
Degrees of freedom are used in the analysis, but the study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
The study tests ridge-tuning dependence, but does not test whether label noise or variance drives peaks, whether peaks split, or whether multiple descent occurs.
The paper does not compare a second-descent curve with an ordinary U-shaped curve using an effective parameter count.
